161	
162	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
163	
164	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
165	
166	## The gap ledger
167	
168	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
169	
170	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
171	
172	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
173	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
174	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
175	
176	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
177	
178	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
179	
180	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
181	
182	## Reading the record
183	
184	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
185	
186	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
187	
188	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
189	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
190	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
191	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
192	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
193	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
194	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
195	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
196	
197	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
198	
199	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
200	
201	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
202	
203	## Writing to the record
204	
205	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
206	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
207	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
208	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
209	  - what it means for the work;
210	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
211	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
212	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
213	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
214	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
215	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
216	
217	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
218	
219	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
220	
221	To add a row:
222	
223	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
224	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
225	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
226	
227	To change a row:
228	
229	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
230	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
231	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
232	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
233	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
234	
235	## The repository's history
236	
237	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
238	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
239	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
240	- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
241	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
242	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
243	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
244	# Exploring: a question that the record does not settle
245	
246	The record keeps what earlier workers found, and they met many of the same questions. Workers have called a thing absent or new when the record already held it.
247	
248	## The choices that are yours
249	
250	The curator settles every conflict and every question about a decision of the curator. Any other choice is yours only if it meets all four of these conditions:
251	
252	- It changes only one area.
253	- It changes no line of the model program.
254	- It changes no decision of the curator.
255	- It can be undone.
256	
257	## Weighing the sources
258	
259	The type group is the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, from 2009 to 2012. Where their late positions disagree with the specification's earlier text, the late positions weigh more. These positions are:
260	
261	- the exclusion rule;
262	- compiled code specialised to each instantiation of a generic, which they kept;
263	- the compiled number tower, which they flattened in 2009 and 2010;
264	- the 2012 write-up on the Return Type Rule (`Papers/Types/journal/`);
265	- the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`).
266	
267	The team's later work is outside the original tree. It is in these places:
268	
269	- `research/extracts/`: the POPL 2019 paper, Steele's talks of 2015 and 2016, and the project's web sites with the post of July 2012 that ended the project;
270	- the reading of the team's 2012 patents: `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md`.
271	
272	If a conflict or a decision not taken needs the designers' reason for a rule, print the row of its design area. WORD is a word of the area, such as `coercion`, `juxtaposition`, `dispatch` or `Arrays`. A word can match several rows, each about 1 to 2 KB.
273	
274	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#The map, by design area@WORD'
275	
276	Then open the sources that the row names. Among them are the `\note{}` boxes and the team's written rationale in the Internal Document appendix: `Specification/appendices/FAQ.tex` and `future.tex`. The row also names the later works that speak to its area, after the words "after the repository (§7)". To read what one of them covers and does not cover, print its row of the map's section "After the repository". WORD is a word of its title, such as `Polymorphic`, `patents`, `JuliaCon` or `Wrapping`. A row is about 1 to 2 KB.
277	
278	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#After the repository@WORD'
279	
280	When your report describes the team's sources on a question, say which of them is one of the late positions above. If the question is about a type rule, also name each later work that you checked.
281	
282	## The procedure
283	
284	1. Search the record with the queries in `records.md`. If two of the team's sources disagree, look for the construct in `revival-changes.md` before you search the record.
285	2. If the record or `revival-changes.md` settles the question, go back to building. Cite what settles it.
286	3. If you have evidence against a decision of the curator, read its POSITIONS entry and the notes that it names. If the decision used your evidence, go back to building.
287	4. Search the original tree. These help: the feature table and the phase map (`compiler.md`, "Before an edit"), the `\note{}` boxes and the map of design areas ("Weighing the sources" above), and the history of a file (`records.md`, "The repository's history").
288	5. Before you write that something does not exist, search the record for it, INDEX included (`index:WORDS`).
289	6. Decide whose choice it is, by "The choices that are yours" above.
290	7. Record each defect that you found as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says. If you make the choice and repair the defect, that is its item 1. If the question stays open, it is its item 3. Record a finding that is not a defect, such as a fact about the original tree, as `records.md`, "Writing to the record", says.
291	8. If your brief does not let you edit the ledger, put the ledger row in your report:
292	   1. Write the row in a file, in the form that `records.md` gives for a new row.
293	   2. Run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py check --rows FILE`. It counts the `?` in the number cell as a broken rule. Correct the row until the check names no other rule.
294	   3. Copy the row into your report.
295	9. If the question touches a passage of the specification, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
296	10. If the choice is yours, make it. Report it as a decision.
297	11. If the choice is the curator's, report it as a decision not taken. Give these:
298	    - the question;
299	    - each source, and its date ("Weighing the sources" above says what else to note);
300	    - each possible solution, and what it changes;
301	    - which solution keeps the current behaviour.
302	12. If you cannot get some evidence in your task, say in your report what is missing and how to get it.

<!-- How numerals and string literals become values on each path, and how that meets `=`, `SEQV`, dispatch, generics and printing: the complement of the strings report, at the curator's request of 07:5x UTC on 2026-11-08, by an Opus worker for the coordinator. Read-only; measured at `157323e5`; its programs, prototypes and draft rows were scratch and are not kept. -->

# Literals: how they become values, and how they meet equivalence

**Base, tools and files.** I read `/home/user/fortress-base28` at `157323e5` and `main` at `cb51060d`. Walk runs used `old-fortress.sh` on base28 with a private caches folder. Compiled runs used a worktree seeded at `157323e5` (`/home/user/fortress-literals`). Three prototypes ran outside both trees. I have removed the worktree and every caches folder. Nothing was built, edited or committed in `/home/user/fortress` or base28, and `git status` is clean in both. The programs, prototypes, results and draft rows are in `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/literals/`. Java paths are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`. I took the row 364 probe's measurements as findings and did not run them again.

## 1. What the sources say

### 1.1 The specification (`Specification/`)

- **Integer numerals.** The Working Draft gives a numeral the types `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`, `Literal[\v\]` and `Numeral[\n,m,r,v\]` (`basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`). No library declares these types. The revival's box says that the library gives every numeral without a radix point the type `IntLiteral`, which extends `Number` and which each integer type, `QQ` and `RR64` coerce from (`:149-165`, P-76). `IntLiteral` is in the text only because of that revision.
- **Float (compound) numerals.** "A numeral is simple if it does not contain a '.' character; otherwise ... compound" (`basic/lexical-structure.tex:1146-1147`). The text says these points:
  - Their type is `RadixPointNumeral[\n,m,10,v\]` (`literals.tex:110-129`).
  - They "are actually rational literals; thus 3.125 has the rational value 3125/1000" (`:179-180`).
  - "Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types because ... we expect them to be polymorphic ... converting it immediately to a floating-point number may lose precision" (`:132-141`).
  - "Library define coercions from numerals to integers (for simple numerals) and rational numbers (for compound numerals)" (`:146-148`).
  - The revised numbers chapter names the coercion into `RR64` "from integer numerals" only (`basic-lib/numbers.tex:43`).

  **So: is `FloatLiteral` part of the specification? No.** The text names it only in Appendix I: in the list of natives (`appendices/changes.tex:4673-4674`) and as a departure of the interpreter (`:4045-4048`). The revision gave no type to compound numerals. That is a gap in the revision.
- **String literals.** Four statements bear on them:
  - "A string literal has type String" (`literals.tex:57`).
  - "Literals are values; they do not require evaluation" (`:25-26`).
  - `String` is among the "simple standard types for literals", and "Values of these types are immutable" (`basic/types-vals-vars.tex:572-581`). Which types "these types" covers is not clear.
  - "The only operation on literals that produces a new literal ... is concatenation ... "foo"||"bar" yields "foobar"" (`basic/expressions/constant.tex:81-85`).
- **Kinds of objects** (`basic/objects.tex`):
  - "numeric literals ... are value objects" (`:41-46`).
  - "Value objects with the same type, environment and fields are indistinguishable" (`:38-39`).
  - "A new object reference is created whenever a reference object is constructed" (`:51-53`).
  - "Reference objects include strings" (`:55-56`). This is the revival's text (P-168), in its box `revival-object-kinds`.
  - Strict equivalence: different dynamic types give `false`; value objects compare field by field and binary words by their bits; references compare by identity (`:435-460`).
- **Static arguments and identity of types.**
  - `id(3)` "instantiates `id` at the numeral's own type" (`basic/inference.tex:183-187`, revival text).
  - A type parameter that only numerals fix, where the conversions tie, becomes `ZZ32` (`:299-317`).
  - Two types are identical only if their names and static arguments are identical (`types-vals-vars.tex:51-52`).
  - A numeral at an `Any` parameter is not coerced: coercion happens only where the parameter type "is exactly the type U" (`basic/conversions-coercions.tex:93-97`).

### 1.2 The team's later word, and the papers

- **The 2012 restart, new evidence.** `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Expressions/literals.tick` (copyright 2012) says:
  - "A literal denotes a fixed, unchanging value." (`:14`)
  - "The type of a string literal is `String`." (`:24`)
  - "The type of a numeric literal is `QQ` if it contains a '.' character, and otherwise is `NN`." (`:25`)
  - "All literals represent value objects; therefore their values do not have object identity." (`:29`)

  No note of the record cites this file: a grep of `explorations/`, `research/` and `.claude/` for `literals.tick` finds nothing. The strings-under-`SEQV` review read only `values.tick:39-56` and called the restart silent on strings. P-25 limits the restart's authority to its Types chapter, so how much weight this file has is the curator's decision. The restart is not consistent with itself: its `types.tick:970-976` still has the old `Numeral[\n,m,r,v\]` text.
- **The type group's prelude, 2009 to 2012.** This is the later word that P-26 names. It declares `trait FloatLiteral excludes {RR32, RR64}`, and `RR64` and `RR32` each declare `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:932`, `:993`, `:996`). It also declares `IntLiteral` as a type apart (`:883`). Its `===` over strings is `a=b` (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:68`).
- **The papers.** `Papers/` says nothing about numeral types or string identity. A grep for "numeral" and "literal" finds only grammar rows and boolean literals.

### 1.3 The library as the team wrote it, and where the code comes from

- **The interpreter's library** declares `value object FloatLiteral extends RR64` (`LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:44`). Climb batch 27 added `value` (`598331c0`). Before P-76, this library declared its integer numeral type as an object that extends `ZZ32` (`changes.tex:3749-3752`). So the float side still has the design that P-76 replaced on the integer side. I cannot trace who wrote the `FloatLiteral` line: the clone is shallow (95 commits; `a874948ac` does not resolve), and no note of the record holds it.
- **The team's tests.** Two of them pin behaviour that this report measures:
  - `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss:16` (2008/2010) asserts that a float numeral prints its whole written text: `"" 3.1415926535897932384000000000001`.
  - `tests/sequivTest.fss` (2008) asserted `equiv(b,c)` for `b: RR64 = 45.0` and `c: RR64 = 5.0 + 40.0`, and `equiv((a,b),(a,c))`. Batch 27 changed these lines to `nequiv` (`:58`, `:94`; diff of `598331c0`).
- **The string objects.** `FlatString`, `CatString` and `SubString` are not declared `value`. `EmptyString` is (`Library/String.fss:282`). The team's walk and its prelude compared strings by their text (the strings review, section 3). `compiler_regressions/seqv.fss:22` asserts `"cat"==="cat"`.

## 2. What each path does today (measured)

The walk programs are `LitStrWalk`, `LitNumWalk`, `LitFloatText`, `LitFloatSame`, `LitQQWalk` and `LitStrShape`, run with `old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base28 <scratch>/caches P.fss`. The compiled programs are `LitComp` and `LitCompArith`, run with `../bin/fortress compile` and `run` against the prelude. On the compiled path, `sEq` is a program-side binding of `equality.sEquiv`, the helper that P-168 names.

### 2.1 String literals

- **How each path makes one.**
  - Walk: `Evaluator.forStringLiteralExpr` returns `FString.make(x.getText())`, a new object at every evaluation (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:1018-1020`; `values/FString.java:40-42`). `FString.seqv` answers `false`, so equivalence is identity (`:35-38`).
  - Compiled: the code generator emits `ldc` and then `FJavaString.make`, a new wrapper at every evaluation (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:5268-5277`; `runtimeValues/FJavaString.java:21`). `equalityRule` compares the wrappers by reference (`nativeHelpers/equalityRule.java:33`, `:62`).
- **Walk results:**

      S1 two occurrences: SEQV false; = true
      S2 one occurrence evaluated twice: SEQV false
      S3 literal vs computed: SEQV false; = true
      S4 typed binding vs a second literal: SEQV false; with itself true
      S9 VCell of two literals: SEQV false; = false

- **Compiled results:**

      C1 two literal occurrences sEquiv false; === true; = true
      C2 one occurrence twice sEquiv false
      C3 literal vs computed sEquiv false; === true

4. Compiled, a numeral at an `Any` parameter is an `IntLiteral` or `FloatLiteral`: `3 === z` is `false` (C6), while walk answers `true` (N1). Detail: §2.2.

**Questions for the curator** (decisions not taken):
1. **String literals.** S-b (intern, keep P-168), S-c (value strings; the restart, `literals.tick:29`), or S-a (keep the accepted cost). Today's behaviour is S-a. The sources are listed in §1.1 and §1.2, with their dates.

4. **The record's wording** of changes 39, 41 and 42, F-326 and `sequivTest:58/:94`. It follows from questions 1 and 2.

## Summary

Each path turns a literal into a value by its own code. Walk makes a new `FString` for every evaluation of a string literal. It gives an integer numeral the class `Int`, `Long` or `BigNum` by its magnitude. It keeps a float numeral as a `FloatLiteral`, which carries its text. The compiled path wraps each string literal in a new `FJavaString`. It boxes numerals as `FIntLiteral` and `FFloatLiteral`, which the checker types as `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral`.

How this meets equivalence:
- **Strings.** `"ab" SEQV "ab"` is `false` on both paths, even for one literal evaluated twice. `=` compares text. Generics are made at `FlatString` under walk and at `String` compiled. An empty string's `SEQV` depends on where it came from.
- **Integers.** Under walk `3 SEQV z` is `true`. Compiled it is `false`, which is the specification's answer.
- **Floats.** Under walk, `y: RR64 = 0.5` stays a `FloatLiteral`, so it is not `SEQV` a computed `0.5`, and neither are value objects that hold it. Compiled, it converts today. After the switch-over it will not, by reading, because the one library declares `FloatLiteral` below `RR64`. Walk prints a numeral's text, so two `SEQV` values print `2.5` and `2.50`. `q: QQ = 0.5` is refused.

**Against the specification:**
- Float numerals are not converted at typed places (`literals.tex:132-148`).
- `QQ` does not coerce from a compound numeral.
- `SEQV` values print differently (`objects.tex:38-39`).
- Walk makes generics at `Int` (row 364).

**`FloatLiteral` is not in the specification.** The revision gave compound numerals no type.

**Against expectation, but not against the specification:**
- Literal strings are not `SEQV`. The text does not say whether a literal is one object, and "Literals are values; they do not require evaluation" leans toward one.
- `3 SEQV z` is `false` compiled.

**New evidence.** The 2012 restart (`literals.tick:14-29`) says: "All literals represent value objects; therefore their values do not have object identity". It also says a numeral with a '.' is a `QQ`. No note of the record cites it.

**Changes 39, 41 and 42** record these representation choices as if the language gave them. In change 39, the literal-string sentence is placed beside the cases it says to assert as correct. Change 41's example rests on the float representation. Change 42 says no row holds the float `false`, while Appendix I calls it a departure. Change 40 records a walk defect, with its row. Changes 43 and 44 are not the pattern.

**The main ways:**
- **S-b:** intern string literals and keep P-168. Measured on prototypes: walk about 3 lines; compiled about 4 lines (Java `==` on the carried string) or about 15 lines (an intern table). No measured test flips, and the team's `seqv.fss:22` passes again.

The probe's programs, `R364*.fss`, were scratch and are not kept. Nothing in `/home/user/fortress` or `/home/user/fortress-base28` was changed or built.

Each probe ran under walk through `old-fortress.sh` with the per-call setup. No fix was built, so every claim about what a fix would do is marked "(by reading)".

`R364A.fss` (rc=0). It declares `object Cell[\T extends Any\](v: T)` and the overloads `kind(Cell[\ZZ32\])`, `kind(Cell[\RR64\])`, `kind(Any)`:

### 1. Where walk instantiates at a run-time class

**The source of the class.** `FValue.type()` of a `ZZ32` value is `value object Int extends ZZ32` (`LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:127`), returned by `FNativeObject.java:38-40`. The traits pair with the objects as follows (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`):

**The sites.**
1. **Generic functions, constructors and generic dotted methods.** All go through `EvaluatorBase.inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction` (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java:72-94`). It reads the value's type at four places:

2. **Reductions and comprehensions with no declared type.** `Evaluator.bigOperatorByElements` (`Evaluator.java:799-815`) calls `__elemsOf`. That builds each element with `__ElemsOne(x)` through `__elemsOne(x: Any)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1428`, object at `:1408`): a constructor inference from the class. `__elemsJoin` (`:1411`) joins them, and `EvaluatorBase.elementsType` (`:267-271`) hands the join to the big operator.

**Not a site.** An untyped array literal is refused: "Can't infer element type for array construction" (`LHSEvaluator.java:145`).

**A. Inference reads a number value at its trait.** This is possible before the switch-over.

content.content:
# Literals in revived Fortress: one picture

## The shape the curator saw

Strict equivalence, `SEQV` (also `===` or `≣`), asks "one value?", not "same text?". Three cases surprised him:

```
"ab" SEQV "ab"            (* false on both paths *)
y: RR64 = 0.5
x: RR64 = 0.25 + 0.25
y SEQV x                  (* false under walk *)
z: ZZ32 = 3
3 SEQV z                  (* walk true, compiled false *)
```

One cause: each path lets its storage of a literal decide what a program sees.
- Strings: each evaluation makes a new object, on both paths.
- Floats: the interpreter's library puts its numeral type below `RR64`; a typed place converts nothing.
- Integers: walk stores `3` as its class `Int`; `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\Int\]`, apart from `Cell[\ZZ32\]`.

He named it "the representation of literals" and "the interpreter's internals leaking out to user land". The fix: one rule on both paths.

## The rule, for every kind of literal

1. **A literal names one value, fixed by its text.** Each evaluation gives that value.
2. **Its type holds that value exactly.** `String` holds every text. No number type holds every numeral (`ZZ32` misses `3000000000`, `RR64` misses `0.1`), so a numeral has its own type: `IntLiteral` (P-76), or `FloatLiteral` with a radix point (P-172).
3. **It converts once, where a type is fixed**, by the library's conversions. Elsewhere it keeps its own type.
4. **`SEQV` and `=` follow the value** (P-168). Values of two types are never `SEQV`. Numbers compare by value; a string by being the same object. `=` is each type's own equality.
5. **An expression of literals alone is a literal.** The team's Working Draft of 2011 folds `"foo" || "bar"` and computes numeral arithmetic exactly: "at most one floating-point rounding error".

## Where the kinds differ by nature

- A number is a value object, with no identity; a string a reference object, with one (P-168). Rule 1 serves both: one literal text is one object (P-171).
- A string converts into no other type; a numeral into several. Strings are not the odd one: their own type is a library type.

## Where a literal converts

A place fixes a type when it declares one: a typed binding or assignment, a parameter, a field, a return type, a written static argument.

A parameter of type `Any` fixes none, nor does a static argument that only the literal fixes: `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\IntLiteral\]`. The coercion chapter agrees.

Where an integer numeral's conversions tie, it reads as `ZZ32`, or wider by size; no float rule exists.

- Compiled today: the checker converts at typed places.
- Walk today: no static types; it converts by the run-time value (P-59). Its float numeral is below `RR64`; its integer numeral is a `ZZ32`.
- After the switch-over: one library (P-37); walk runs the checker and uses its conversions (P-12).

## `SEQV` and `=` after the two decisions

Strings (P-171):
```
b = "b"
"ab" SEQV ("a" || "b")    (* true: folded *)
"ab" SEQV ("a" || b)      (* false: built at run time *)
"ab" = ("a" || b)         (* true *)
```

Floats (P-172):
```
y SEQV x                  (* true *)
0.5 SEQV x                (* false: FloatLiteral, RR64 *)
0.5 = x                   (* true *)
```

Integers (P-76), compiled today:
```
3 SEQV z                  (* false: IntLiteral, ZZ32 *)
3 = z                     (* true *)
```

## The team's sources

They agree: a literal denotes one fixed value (the Working Draft, the 2012 restart); a string literal is a `String`; a numeral has its own type, converted by the library (the draft and the compiler's library, the later word, P-26).

Uneven in four places:
- Three numeral designs: own type, converted (draft, compiler); below a default, `FloatLiteral extends RR64` (interpreter's library); `QQ` or `NN` (restart).
- The compiler's `IntLiteral` is a `Number`, its `FloatLiteral` not; it has no `QQ`.
- No source says whether a string literal is one object.
- The draft folds strings and numerals; the team built only the integer fold, on the compiled path.

The papers say nothing.

## What is not yet uniform

- **Float ties.** `1.0 s`, for `s: ZZ32`, fits `QQ`'s and `RR64`'s product by conversion; a float tie rule, `RR64`, picks one.
- **Float folds.** Without rule 5, `(0.25 + 0.25) SEQV 0.5` is false.
- **Printing and rounding.** `2.5` and `2.50` are `SEQV` but print apart; `round` rounds the double. The float decision left both open; rule 1 says: the exact value.
- **Walk's types.** Walk builds generics at `Int` and `FlatString`; he asked for a fix now.
- **Walk's integer numeral** is a `ZZ32` until walk runs the checker.

**The one fork** is a place that fixes no type. Does a numeral keep its own type there, or take a default, as in Swift? He took "keeps it" for floats (P-172). The rule asks the same for integers, as the integer decision says: `3 SEQV z` is false. His words of 08:03 lean to a default; his rule of 12:36 named only typed places. A default for integers alone splits the numeral kinds; for both, it reverses a clause of the float decision. No team source asks for it.

## The plan

Seven rungs, sized by reading; tests on both paths unless marked.
1. **One object per string literal** (P-171): walk interns; both paths compare the carried Java strings by `==`; a shared phase folds `||` of two literals. About 3 and 4 lines; fold not sized. Asserts the string lines.
2. **`FloatLiteral` apart** (P-172): `QQ`, `RR64`, `RR32` convert from it, with their `=`; ties read `RR64`; compiled numerals round once. 15 to 30 library lines; the rest not sized. Asserts `q: QQ = 0.5`, `1/2 = 0.5`, `Cell(0.5)` a `Cell[\FloatLiteral\]`, `1.0 s` an `RR64`.
3. **Walk converts a `FloatLiteral` at each typed place** and breaks float ties. About 20 lines. Asserts `y SEQV x`, walk.
4. **Walk shows only language types**: inference reads `Int` as `ZZ32` and its strings as `String`; messages print traits. 40 to 50 lines for numbers, the rest not sized. Asserts `Just(z) = Just[\ZZ32\](z)`, and `Cell("s")` a `Cell[\String\]`, walk.
5. **A float numeral prints and rounds by its value.** Not sized. Asserts `"" 2.50 = "2.5"`; the team's print test passes. Needs his word.
6. **Numeral expressions fold exactly**, in a shared phase. Not sized. Asserts `(0.25 + 0.25) SEQV 0.5`. Needs his word.
7. **Walk's integer numeral becomes an `IntLiteral`** once walk runs the checker (P-12). Asserts `3 SEQV z` false, walk. Done early, a probe failed 24 passing tests, 9 for want of static types (F-74).

## The switch-over and microGPT

- At the last gate the distance to the switch-over is 0 errors, the checker count 0 (F-53). Rung 2 and the folds of rungs 1 and 6 change what the checker reads, so both stages measure them.
- The switch-over should follow rung 2; else the compiled path takes `FloatLiteral` below `RR64`, and `y SEQV x` turns false.
- No line of microGPT changes if float ties read `RR64`. Else, by reading, `1 - beta1`, `beta1^t` and `1.0 s` tie (flat lines 77 to 82, APL lines 106 and 112). Neither program uses `SEQV`.

## Where the coordinator's framing departed from what the curator asked

**What he asked for**, in chat at 08:03 UTC, after his page comments of 07:20 and 07:51:
- "I'm seeing a pattern that the literals are interfering with equivalence in a way that's surprising to me."
- "why would the compiler's representation of literals in the source code not directly convert into the value type so that they are all equivalent?"
- "if the declarations are inferred ... as just a string, they should be interchangeable from the user's point of view."
- "we need a complementary [study] that ... tries to resolve the internal representation of literals ... numeric literals and string literals."
- Of the skill's changes 39 to 44: "I was getting the feeling that this is the same pattern, which gives me wrong vibes."
- On the page: "I didn't want the interpreter's internals leaking out to user land"; "it is still worth fixing ... the behavior of the interpreter now".

**What the brief asked the worker for**, at 08:04:
- It quoted his words almost whole, and asked one question for all literals.
- Its deliverable split them: "list every way forward ... for numerals and for string literals apart"; "Name each finding that would change a decision of the curator's, and give options for those only."
- It did not ask what the three cases share, or for one rule.

**What the study gave**, at 08:39:
- Each kind measured on both paths, and the skill's pattern found: three of changes 39 to 44, and a fourth in its example, record one path's behaviour as if the language gave it.
- 17 ways in three groups, strings, floats and integers, weighed per kind. Its summary keeps the split.

**Where the three asks departed**, at 11:58, 12:26 and 13:25:
- They were asks 1 to 3 of seven, one per kind. Each was a menu, with keeping today's behaviour among the options.
- Ask 1 moved strings in generics, `Cell("s")` a `Cell[\FlatString\]`, to "the row 364 ask", the ask on walk's generics. Ask 3 was that ask, and it left strings out.
- The float clause for a place that fixes no type came from the coordinator: ask 2 ("exact where nothing is declared") and its reply of 12:37 ("Where nothing fixes a type, as in `Cell(0.5)`, it stays exact"). He accepted it: "I think we are aligned on 1A". His own words named only `QQ` and floats of fixed size.
- Ask 3 came after a compaction. It did not say that this clause settles the integer case. It offered a default type for integers alone, which splits the numeral kinds, and did not say so.
- Ask 3 offered "No walk fix now" as option 1a, though at 07:51 the coordinator had agreed with him: "Fixing walk is the right move."
- He answered asks 1 and 2 with principles, not options: "If I was implementing this, I would ..."; "I don't know which design ... achieves this from the options that you offered, but that is my reading of the intention behind the specification's word." The coordinator mapped each back onto an option.

**His complaint**, at 14:21: "I wanted a holistic re-evaluation of the literals, and I'm getting piecewise proposal for fixes, and I'm not seeing the unified holistic vision that I was asking for."

**What his words changed above:**
- The shape is stated in his words: the representation of literals, and internals leaking.
- Rung 4 is his request of 07:51, and its string half his words of 08:03. Neither is offered as an option.
- The fork sets his two statements side by side: a numeral "directly" in "the value type" (08:03), and exact until a fixed-size type (12:36).

## Appendix A: citations and detail

**The record's reviews.** The study, `explorations/reviews/literals-2026-11-08.md`: measurements S1, S2, C1, C2 (strings), N1, C6 (`3 SEQV z`), N4, C7 (floats), E1 (`2.5`, `2.50`). The probe of walk's generics, `explorations/reviews/row-364-walk-generics-2026-11-08.md`: R364A, R364I, way A, `LongStringTests.fss:121`, `:141`. The strings review, `explorations/reviews/string-equivalence-2026-11-06.md`. The scout's file of his words, `literals-recovery/evidence.md` in the scratchpad.

**Specification.**
- Working Draft, `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex`: `:25-26` "Literals are values"; `:31-33` `BooleanLiteral[\true\]`; `:40` `Character`; `:57` `String`; `:132-148` numerals "not directly converted", "their own types", library coercions; `:163` "3.125 has the rational value 3125/1000"; `:173` "at most one floating-point rounding error".
- `Specification/basic/expressions/constant.tex`: `:44-74` literal, constant and static traits; `:81-87` concatenation makes a new literal; `:90-92` every literal is a constant.
- Revised `literals.tex:149-165`: the `IntLiteral` box, the chapter's one revision. The text of the string and float decisions is not written yet: no `FloatLiteral` in `Specification/` outside Appendix I.
- Appendix I, "Which objects are value objects": its Effect names walk's float numeral at `RR64` and the integer split as departures.
- `basic/objects.tex:24-56`: the kinds of objects; "numeric literals" are value objects.
- `basic/conversions-coercions.tex:98-101`: coercion only where the declared type "is exactly the type U".
- `basic/inference.tex:183-187`: `id(3)` "at the numeral's own type"; `:299-317`: a tied integer numeral reads as `ZZ32`.
- The 2012 restart, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Expressions/literals.tick:14-29`. P-25 gives the restart weight for its Types chapter only.

**Libraries and code** (Java under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`).
- Compiler's library: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:883` `IntLiteral extends { Number, Equality[\IntLiteral\] }`; `:996` `trait FloatLiteral excludes {RR32, RR64}`; `:932`, `:993` its coercions; `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:68` strings' `===` by `=`.
- Interpreter's library: `LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:44` `value object FloatLiteral extends RR64`; `:127` `value object Int extends ZZ32`; `:199` `IntLiteral`; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:291-297` `RR64 comprises { Float, FloatLiteral }`; `:395-404` `QQ` converts from `IntLiteral`, not `FloatLiteral`. Its earlier integer numeral type extended `ZZ32`, its arithmetic held back "until coercion is implemented" (Appendix I, "revival-numeral-type").
- Checker: `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:461-480` types literals `String`, `Character`, `IntLiteral`, `FloatLiteral`, `Boolean`. The team's integer fold, 2012: `compiler/desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java`, compiled only.
- Walk: `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:1018-1020`, a new `FString` per evaluation; `:1631-1637`, `FFloatLiteral` with its text, `FIntLiteral.make` to `Int`, `Long` or `BigNum`. Compiled: `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:2035`, `:4207`, `:5268`.

**The float tie, by reading.** After rung 2, `QQ` and `RR64` each convert from `FloatLiteral` and from `ZZ32`, and `QQ` excludes `RR64`. So `1.0 s`, `1 - beta1` and `beta1^t` find two declarations, neither more specific: "Ambiguous coercion". A tie given to `QQ` would make `beta1^t` an exact rational. A numeral tie on these lines stopped the checker before: `10.0^(-5)` (F-58, row 533). `beta1`, `beta2`, `lr0` and `epsilon_A` are bound without a type (flat `:18`, APL `:27`), so they stay `FloatLiteral` and convert at each use: a few times a step, outside the element loops (flat `:77-79`).

**Measured for this page.** `javac` and `java` on `literals-recovery/powcheck/PowCheck.java` in the scratchpad: `Math.pow(10.0, -5.0) == 1e-5`, `(10.0, -8.0) == 1e-8` and `(10.0, 10.0) == 1e10` print `true`; `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` prints `false`. So rung 6 keeps microGPT's three numeral powers on today's bits, and changes `0.1 + 0.2`.

**Rungs.**
- 1: the study's prototypes, protoS (walk, about 3 lines; 51 walk tests unchanged) and protoC (compiled, about 4); the team's `compiler_regressions/seqv.fss:22` passes again.
- 2: the study's ways F-b (`FloatLiteral` apart) and F-e (`QQ` converts from it): 10 to 20 lines, and 5 to 10 for the exact `QQ` helper. One rounding ends the compiled path's two or three (F-304).
- 3: the study's way F-d (walk converts at declared places), about 20 lines in `LHSEvaluator` and the parameter binding. P-172 names binding, parameter and field; the rule adds assignment and return. It flips `StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk.fss:32`, `sequivTest.fss:58` and `:94` back to the team's `equiv`, and F-326's walk sentence.
- 4: the probe's way A (inference reads the five number classes at their traits) and sub-choice S (the string objects at `String`); messages at the probe's `FType.toString` sites; three `TupleOrder*Refused.test` keys move. Until rung 7, walk's `Cell(3)` is then a `Cell[\ZZ32\]`, the revised text's interim answer.
- 5: `values/FFloatLiteral.java:26-33` prints the text. The shortest exact decimal keeps `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss:16`, which has no trailing zero. PLAN's default is the team's printing (`PLAN.md:155`).
- 6: the Working Draft's static rational expressions; it can move the integer fold to a shared phase too.
- 7: walk cannot yet run the checker: it has no case for the checker's conversion nodes (F-9). ## Appendix B: the record's entries on literals and equivalence

Fetch each with `facts-extract.sh 'P-n+'` and `'history:P-n'`. "History" marks a history that holds his words or a reversal. A scan of `FACTS-history.md` finds his words in no FACTS entry below.

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
number types (\secref{literals}).
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
value does not fit in the narrower type.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values.

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
is a static error.

One way to think about coercion is that if type \VAR{T} can be coerced
to type \VAR{U}, then a value of type \VAR{T} can be used to ``stand
in'' for a value of type \VAR{U} in a functional call, for example.  This is
different from actually \emph{being} of type \VAR{U}; it means only
that, given any value of type \VAR{T}, an appropriate value of type
\VAR{U} can be computed to substitute for it.  Also, coercion occurs
only when the declared type of the corresponding parameter in the
functional declaration is exactly the type \VAR{U} being coerced to

#!/bin/bash # runlist.sh : runs each walk test of the list under the prototype's classes L=/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/literals W=/home/user/fortress-literals P=$1; LIST=$2; OUT=$3 cd $W export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH export FORTRESS_HOME=$W FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$W/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$W/tmp" unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1) export FORTRESS_CACHES=$L/$P/caches cd ProjectFortress/tests : > $OUT for t in $(cat $LIST); do if [ "$P" = base ]; then CPX="$CP"; else CPX="$L/$P/classes:$CP"; fi o=$(timeout 150 java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$FORTRESS_CACHES -cp "$CPX" com.sun.fortress.Shell $t.fss 2>&1); rc=$? f=$(echo "$o" | grep -m1 -E 'FAIL|Error|error|Exception' | cut -c1-220) echo "$t rc=$rc $f" >> $OUT done echo DONE >> $OUT 3:**Base, tools and files.** I read `/home/user/fortress-base28` at `157323e5` and `main` at `cb51060d`. Walk runs used `old-fortress.sh` on base28 with a private caches folder. Compiled runs used a worktree seeded at `157323e5` (`/home/user/fortress-literals`). Three prototypes ran outside both trees. I have removed the worktree and every caches folder. Nothing was built, edited or committed in `/home/user/fortress` or base28, and `git status` is clean in both. The programs, prototypes, results and draft rows are in `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/literals/`. Java paths are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`. I took the row 364 probe's measurements as findings and did not run them again. 53:- **The string objects.** `FlatString`, `CatString` and `SubString` are not declared `value`. `EmptyString` is (`Library/String.fss:282`). The team's walk and its prelude compared strings by their text (the strings review, section 3). `compiler_regressions/seqv.fss:22` asserts `"cat"==="cat"`. 57:The walk programs are `LitStrWalk`, `LitNumWalk`, `LitFloatText`, `LitFloatSame`, `LitQQWalk` and `LitStrShape`, run with `old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base28 /caches P.fss`. The compiled programs are `LitComp` and `LitCompArith`, run with `../bin/fortress compile` and `run` against the prelude. On the compiled path, `sEq` is a program-side binding of `equality.sEquiv`, the helper that P-168 names. 63: - Compiled: the code generator emits `ldc` and then `FJavaString.make`, a new wrapper at every evaluation (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:5268-5277`; `runtimeValues/FJavaString.java:21`). `equalityRule` compares the wrappers by reference (`nativeHelpers/equalityRule.java:33`, `:62`). 104: So against a typed `ZZ32` the paths split: walk answers `true`, the compiled path `false`. The compiled `false` is the specification's answer, because a numeral at `Any` keeps its own type. Appendix I already names this split (`changes.tex:4048-4051`). 129: Today the compiled path answers `true` where walk answers `false`. After the switch-over, the checker reads the one library's `FloatLiteral` below `RR64` and inserts no coercion. So by reading, the compiled path will then answer `false` as walk does. Climb batch 27's planner said the same (`CLIMB-BATCH-27.md`, fork E1). 132: - The compiled path prints `0.5` for `y2` (C9), and throws for a bare numeral (row 362). 160:- **P-168** fixes the rule. Strings are reference objects. Its history records the costs that the curator accepted: `"cat" SEQV "cat"` is `false` for two literals, and `seqv.fss:22` changes. It also records his words "natives should go down to Java `==` to reveal the true nature of the reference types". On the compiled path, Java `==` on the strings that the wrappers carry gives exactly Java's literal answer. The `protoC` prototype measured this (§6.1): `C1 ... sEquiv true`, `C3 ... sEquiv false`. Batch 27 built `==` on the wrapper instead. 182: - "Under walk, each evaluation of a string literal makes a new string, unlike Java ... So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` and `V("ab") = V("ab")` are false." The compiled path does the same (C1, C2), and neither P-168 nor the text requires it. The sentence stands between the two cases that the passage calls "the rule's: assert them as correct". 188:- **Change 42** (`interpreter.md:18`). It records the one library's `FloatLiteral` representation as the rule's answer, says that "no ledger row holds it", and tells workers not to record it. Appendix I calls it a departure, and today's compiled path answers `true`. **Same pattern: yes, most directly.** It describes a departure of walk (and of the compiled path after the switch-over, by reading), stated as if it were the language. 226: - (i) Compare the carried Java strings by `==` in the helper: about 4 lines (prototype `protoC`). It relies on the JVM interning `ldc` strings. A side effect: wherever Java returns the same string object, as `substring(0, length)` returns `this`, two strings that walk keeps apart would be `SEQV` compiled. 250: - Record: file R1, R2 and R3. Walk and, after the switch-over, the compiled path answer `false` against computed values. 273: - Alone, the compiled path after the switch-over is unchanged; it needs F-b. 296: - Tests: compiled tests that rely on `IntLiteral` at `Any` (row 79's compiled answer, row 364's compiled `IntLiteral`). Not counted. 305: - Effect: helps compiled microGPT's library loops, by reading. 319: | ? | under walk a float numeral bound to an `RR64` variable, parameter or field stays a `FloatLiteral`, so it is not `SEQV` a computed `RR64` of the same bits: for `y: RR64 = 0.5` and `x: RR64 = 0.25 + 0.25`, `y SEQV x` is `false`, as is `V(0.5) = V(x)` for `value object V(f: RR64)` | CONTESTED | library gap vs spec (library) | `basic/expressions/literals.tex`, "Literals" | `ProjectFortress/tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk.fss` | review literals-2026-11-08 | siblings: 20, 454. The one library declares `value object FloatLiteral extends RR64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:44` at 157323e5), so no coercion runs; the prelude's `FloatLiteral` excludes `RR64`, which coerces from it (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:932`, `:996`), so compiled `y SEQV x` is `true` until the switch-over. #!/bin/bash
# The gate's distance stage: the compiled checker over the whole interpreter library, the
# fourteen components, the prelude's twelve and the two that List imports, and their apis,
# every stage of every unit run whatever the earlier stages reported, so that nothing hides
# behind an early return; one table.
#
# Why it exists: Pavol's answer 11 (POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-26): the full measurement of the
# distance to the switch-over "becomes a report-only stage of phase 3's gates, whose job is
# driving it down". The checker-count stage beside it (../checker-count/run.sh) sees only
# the errors before each api's early return, 62 of about 1,740 on 2026-09-27.
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir] [setting]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched: the
# shadow sources and classes, the driver, the checker's caches (-Dfortress.caches) and the
# JVM's temporary directory (so Rats! leaves nothing in /tmp) go to the scratch directory
# (default: $TMPDIR or /tmp), and the caches are deleted at the end. It never removes
# /tmp/fortress*rats, which other runs on the machine use. Exit 0 if the table was
# produced, 1 if it could not be. One JVM, -Xmx4g, one busy core: 789 s on the idle 4-CPU
# container on 2026-09-27, 14 to 24 minutes under load 7 to 18 (switch-over-distance-flat.md
# section 5); the table's #seconds and #machine rows say what each run took and where.
#
# The setting: "compile" by default, the compile command's own: DistanceMulti's -setting
# compile takes the extends-Object pre-desugaring from the line that opens
# Shell.useCompilerLibraries() in the tracked ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java,
# read at each run (the run stops, with no total, if that line is not there; its "### order="
# line prints the switch it read, extendsObject=...), and turns the compiled-expression
# desugaring on, as the compile path does. Answer 11 names the compile path's setting. That
# line sets the switch off, the implicit bound Any of P-42 (row 412), so the default runs as
# "any", which fixes the switch off whatever Shell.java says; with the switch on, the compile
# setting gave 685 errors on climb batch 22's code, 580 on the bound Object (F-289). "any"
# differs from walk's setting by the compiled-expression desugaring: on the tree of 2026-09-27
# 1,746 to 1,747 errors against 1,737 to 1,738 (FACTS.md, "The true distance to the
# switch-over"). The third argument, any or walk, runs another setting, for a comparison
# with the measurements on file; the gate never passes it.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false), as in
# every run of the measurement: keyed on declaration pairs, it hides 27 to 35 errors
# depending on the build order (FACTS.md, "The overloading checker's memo hides errors
# by build order, so every count runs with it off ...").
#
# The sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-27, so that the gate does not
# depend on a probe directory, as the checker-count stage's were: DistanceMulti.java from
# perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance-flat/ (35ef70584); shadow-patch.py from
# perf-probes/prelude/desugar-codegen/ (e5d8cdbd2); add-patch.py and errors.py from
# perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance/ (a7e3df9ad, 14d2f9839); classify.py from
# perf-probes/prelude/distance-triage/ (e17a9badc); all unchanged but classify.py, which since
# row 577 finds the library places that name three of its classes by their declarations in
# the tree's sources ($FH, passed to table.py), not by line ranges. table.py is new: it
# counts as those scripts count and prints the rows below. The shadow classes are not
# copies: they are made from the tracked sources at every run by text edits that must each
# match exactly once (shadow-patch.py, add-patch.py), so there is no copied checker to go
# stale silently; an edit that no longer matches stops the run before the checker starts,
# and the table then says so in its #shadow row, with no counts.
#
# The table, tab-separated, every row tagged:
#   #distance   the setting, the switches and the fourteen targets
#   #total      distinct errors; or "none:" and why, when no total was measured, as when a
#               target stopped with errors the stage does not count, such as a parse error,
#               or an api that only a later target checks reported errors (table.py)
#   #kind       by kind (errors.py): exclusion, comprises, overloading, return-type, ...
#   #class      by root cause (classify.py, distance-triage.md section 2), with its name
#   #check      a disagreement: errors.py's and table.py's totals, or sites classify.py cannot
#               find in the tree's library source
#   #unit       by the unit that printed the error first
#   #crash      each declaration, stage or target the checker crashed on
#   #seconds    the run's wall time, and FortressLibrary's, the part that takes it
#   #machine    nproc, CPU model and MHz, load at start, JDK, FORTRESS_THREADS
#   #shadow     whether every shadow edit matched the tracked sources; the last row
# ../distance/compare.sh compares two tables. The run-to-run variation is 2 to 4 errors,
# in the comparisons' and Maybe's pairs and the joins of array bodies (switch-over-
# distance-flat.md section 5).
set -u

OUT=${1:-}
if [ -z "$OUT" ] ; then echo "usage: $0 <out-file> [scratch-dir] [any|walk|compile]" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi
case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$PWD/$OUT" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}

#!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one
fi
FORTRESS_HOME="$BASE" FORTRESS_CACHES="$PRIV" exec "$BASE/bin/fortress" "$@"

1	(* The compiled helper of SEQV answers by the rule of objects.tex, section "Object Equivalence": values of different types are never equivalent, value objects and tuples compare field by field, floats by their bits, and reference objects, strings among them, only with themselves. *)
     2	component StrictEquivalenceRuleCompiled
     3	export Executable
     4	
     5	sEq(a: Any, b: Any): Boolean = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.equality.sEquiv")
     6	
     7	object Pt(x: ZZ32, y: ZZ32) end
     8	value object VPlain(a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32) end
     9	value object CC64(re: RR64, im: RR64) end
    10	object RC64(re: RR64, im: RR64) end
    11	
    12	numbers(): () = do
    13	  i: ZZ32 = 3
    14	  j: ZZ32 = 3
    15	  l: ZZ64 = 3
    16	  r: RR64 = 3.0
    17	  assert(sEq(i, j), "two ZZ32 3s")
    18	  assert(NOT sEq(i, l), "a ZZ32 3 and a ZZ64 3")
    19	  assert(NOT sEq(i, r), "a ZZ32 3 and an RR64 3.0")
    20	  zero: RR64 = 0.0
    21	  nz: RR64 = -0.0
    22	  nan: RR64 = zero / zero
    23	  assert(NOT sEq(zero, nz), "0.0 and -0.0")
    24	  assert(sEq(nan, nan), "a NaN with itself")
    25	end
    26	
    27	tuples(): () = do
    28	  t1: (ZZ32, ZZ32) = (1, 2)
    29	  t2: (ZZ32, ZZ32) = (1, 2)
    30	  a: Any = t1
    31	  b: Any = t2
    32	  assert(sEq(a, b), "two (1,2)")
    33	end
    34	
    35	strings(): () = do
    36	  s1: String = "ab" || "cd"
    37	  s2: String = "abc" || "d"
    38	  assert(NOT sEq(s1, s2), "two strings built apart")
    39	  assert(sEq(s1, s1), "a string with itself")
    40	end
    41	
    42	objects(): () = do
    43	  p = Pt(1, 2)
    44	  q = Pt(1, 2)
    45	  assert(NOT sEq(p, q), "two Pt(1,2)")
    46	  assert(sEq(p, p), "a Pt with itself")
    47	  assert(NOT sEq(VPlain(1, 2), VPlain(1, 3)), "VPlain(1,2) and VPlain(1,3)")
    48	  assert(sEq(VPlain(1, 2), VPlain(1, 2)), "two VPlain(1,2)")
    49	  assert(sEq(CC64(1.0, 2.0), CC64(1.0, 2.0)), "two CC64(1.0, 2.0)")
    50	  assert(NOT sEq(CC64(1.0, 2.0), CC64(1.0, 3.0)), "CC64(1.0, 2.0) and CC64(1.0, 3.0)")
    51	  assert(NOT sEq(RC64(1.0, 2.0), RC64(1.0, 2.0)), "two RC64(1.0, 2.0)")
    52	end
    53	
    54	run(): () = do
    55	  numbers()
    56	  tuples()
    57	  strings()
    58	  objects()

- P-169 **The runtime's own 45 native bindings, the arrays' store, threads with `abort`, the task trace and the numerals, name compiled helpers that walk's loader answers with walk's own operations, P-167's device, in three compiled shapes.** Each keeps P-58's form, a bare `builtinPrimitive("…")` naming a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the compiled path runs; walk's loader answers the name with walk's glue, so walk keeps its `AtomicArray` store, its `spawn` and its numerals, and for these names P-58's walk half bends, as for P-167's two. The arrays' 7, of `PrimitiveArray`, `PrimImmutableArray` and `PrimImmutableRR64Array`: the compiled half by P-164's device, a store trait in `FortressLibrary` whose bindings name helpers of a new `nativeHelpers/arrayOps` over a compiled class that holds the elements; `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` leave the native component and hold the store in a field, and walk's native object below the trait holds an `AtomicArray`; `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s two are on a compiled `double[]` class that no factory chooses until array decision A (P-84, P-85; F-333). The compiled store is an `Object[]`, and the compiled transaction tracks its reads and writes by the array and the index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`): P-84 stores every number type's array unboxed, so a compiled `atomic` write into any array needs that keying, and an array of objects keeps one box an element, not two. Threads, `abort` and the task trace, 6: helpers in a `nativeHelpers` class over the compiled runtime, as the team's `nativeHelpers/runtime.java` is (F-335); `Thread`'s `val`, `wait`, `ready` and `stop` raise until the code generator compiles `spawn` (row 82). The numerals, 32: `IntLiteral`'s 8 conversions and comparisons are Fortress text over its `asZZ` (F-331); the other 24, `IntLiteral`'s 21 and `FloatLiteral`'s 3, name helpers that compute, not the prelude's raising stubs (row 318), at the names batch after a reading review designs their carrier, and walk's loader answers them by one rule per helper class, not by a table of names, still refusing a misspelt name. A test on both paths holds the two halves together where both run; `IntLiteral`'s 21 keep only walk's load check, since no walk numeral is an `IntLiteral` (P-76). Why: every array, vector, varargs list and `args` of the one library is built on `PrimitiveArray` or `PrimImmutableArray`, and a body left on glue compiles to the library's own `builtinPrimitive`, which fails, so by the code's reading a compiled program would raise at its first array; walk's loader carries no element, `Thread` or literal (F-299), and an `Object` carrier would take walk's array writes out of walk's transactions. Detail: `reviews/natives-device-2026-11-07.md`, sections 3.1 to 3.4; the store's shape: `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-28.md`, "The questions for the curator, before the launch", Q2.
- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.
- P-38 **The compiler prelude's own text is not repaired: its defects go with it at the switch-over.** A helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is fixed for the one library, and the prelude's value moves with it (F-313). Its `Maybe` block and its `REM` guard `if other = -1 then 0` stay as landed until the prelude is deleted, and their tests stay. Then the compiled tests respell its reversed wrapping and saturating operators (row 348), `ZZ64`'s compiled shift closes (row 381), and the specification's `shift` reaches the compiled path (row 383). `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is then promoted, and the switch-over batch finds the compiler tests that bind `shift`, a reserved name from then on.

content.content:
\end{description}

\subsection{The type of an integer numeral}
\seclabel{revival-numeral-type}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{literals}; \secref{coercion}.
\item[Change] \secref{literals} says that \library\ give every numeral without a
radix point the type \TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the
number types, and that each of the five integer types, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a coercion from it.
The box of \secref{coercion} says the same of the coercion into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, and that the interpreter does not yet give a numeral that
type.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 29~September 2026 that a numeral has a type of its own, \TYP{IntLiteral},
from which each number type converts, the compiled path's own library's working
version taken in place of the numeral types of \secref{literals}, which no
library declares, and that \library\ take it before the interpreter does, since
the interpreter can give a numeral that type without changing the declarations
its calls reach only once it runs with the static types of the compiled type
checker.
\Library\ declared their numeral type an object extending \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
its arithmetic withheld by the comment ``Do not enable these until coercion is
implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals.''
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss}, lines
495--496 before this change, in the revival's repository).
Coercion is implemented on both paths now, and \library\ declare the type as
the compiled path's own library does
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi}, lines
390--431): beside the number types under \TYP{Number}, with the arithmetic that
comment withheld, each integer type declaring a coercion from it.
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, which that library does not declare from
a numeral, coerce from it too, since \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} coerces from every integer
type (\secref{basic-rationals}) and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} from integer numerals
(\secref{revival-int-float}).
\item[Effect] The compiled type checker converts an integer numeral to the
integer type, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} or \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} that its context expects,
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} among them, which refused a numeral
before.
A numeral beside a value of an integer type is converted to that type where no
declaration of the operator is applicable to the two without coercion, and that
type's own declaration of the operator is then the most specific
(\secref{resolving-coercion}); \library\ state on each integer type the
comparisons \EXP{<}, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{>} and \EXP{\geq}, \OPR{CMP},
\OPR{MAXNUM}, \OPR{MINNUM} and a power with a numeral exponent, which the types
inherited before from a declaration that a converted numeral leaves tied with
those of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
Equality is stated in pairs instead: each integer type declares an \EXP{=}
whose parameter is of type \TYP{IntLiteral}, and \TYP{IntLiteral} one whose
parameter is of each integer type, and each converts the numeral by its
coercion into the integer type and compares by that type's own \EXP{=}.
Inequality is not converted: the top-level declaration of \EXP{\neq}, whose
parameters are of type \TYP{Any}, is applicable to an integer value and a
numeral without coercion, and the compiled type checker selects it and converts
neither operand.
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} states in its api, for the same reason, the additive and
multiplicative operators its body declares.
\TYP{IntLiteral} declares its own \VAR{zero}, \VAR{one}, \VAR{even},
\VAR{odd}, \VAR{floor}, \VAR{ceiling}, \VAR{truncate}, \OPR{DIVIDES},
\OPR{TIMES} and a power with a numeral exponent, which a numeral reached
before as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, since no member of \TYP{Integral} is
applicable to a numeral of that type, even with coercion
(\secref{applicability-with-coercion}).
A numeral given where any integer type is accepted, as the count of a shift,
is converted to the narrowest of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} that holds its value, as \secref{numeral-default} reads a
numeral whose conversions tie.
The interpreter still gives an integer numeral the type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} by its value, so a numeral reaches none
of the declarations of \TYP{IntLiteral} there.
Its calls of the comparisons, \OPR{CMP}, \OPR{MAXNUM} and \OPR{MINNUM} on an
integer type reach that type's own declarations, which answer as the
declarations inherited before did, except that \OPR{MAXNUM} and \OPR{MINNUM}
with a converted argument, which stopped at a tie with those of
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} or answered at \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, now answer at the integer

The departures:
the interpreter gives a floating-point numeral bound to a variable of type

compared with a typed value can answer differently on the two paths;
the compiled path's own library, used until the one library replaces it,
answers \EXP{\sequiv} on values of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64},
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, on strings and on booleans by
\EXP{=} before it
reaches the rule, so there two equal strings built apart are strictly
equivalent and \EXP{0.0} is strictly equivalent to \EXP{-0.0} (row~908 of the

\subsection{The contexts that give a call an expected type}
\seclabel{revival-expected-contexts}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{static-arg-inference}; \secref{numeral-default}.
\item[Change] The list of the contexts in which a call has an expected type,
in \secref{static-arg-inference}, gives the last expression of a block the
block's expected type whether or not local declarations precede it, and gains
two contexts: a clause of an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause,
whose expected type is \TYP{()}, and a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression
that has an expected type, its \KWD{else} clause among them, whose expected
type is that of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
The sentence after the list says that the expected type is used also for a call
written by loose juxtaposition, as \EXP{f\;x}.
A second revision adds a third context to the list: the body of a \KWD{label}
expression that has an expected type, and the \KWD{with} clause expression of
each \KWD{exit} expression whose target is that \KWD{label} expression, whose
expected type is that of the \KWD{label} expression.
A third revision adds a fourth: an argument of a call that the section does not
accept with its arguments typed without an expected type, where the argument is
itself a call with inferred static arguments, whose expected type is
the parameter type at its position of each declaration of the enclosing call in
turn, instantiated, where that declaration has static parameters, by the
arguments not so typed and the expected type of the enclosing call; and a
paragraph after the list says that the enclosing call then invokes, of the
declarations that are applicable to it with its arguments so typed and whose
return types fit its expected type, the one more specific than every other on
the parameter types they declare, and is otherwise typed as before, so that a
declaration that the section accepts for the call as its arguments are typed
without an expected type is never passed over.
The item of the list of what the chapter does not yet describe, in
\secref{numeral-default}, names the body of a \KWD{for} loop, and no longer
names the contexts that the list of contexts now gives, the body of a
\KWD{label} expression and an argument of another call among them.
Each changed passage has a box.
How a call is instantiated under its expected type is unchanged.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
revival's decision of 8~October 2026 that these four contexts give a call the
type that the text already requires of them, a clause of a \KWD{typecase}
expression by the rule for the type of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
The text gives each context its type.
``If there is no \KWD{else} clause in an \KWD{if} expression, then every clause
must have type \EXP{()}'' (\secref{if-expr}).
``If the last element of the expression block is an expression, the value and
type of this expression are the value and type of the expression block as a
whole'' (\secref{block-expr}), whatever local declarations precede it.
The static arguments of an identifier reference ``are statically inferred from
the context of the function call'' (\secref{idn-ref}), however the call is
written.
``The type of a \KWD{typecase} expression is the union of types of all
right-hand sides of the typecase clauses'' (\secref{typecase}), which is a
subtype of the expected type when the type of each clause is.
